title: The Ogre, the Orb, and the Rival Wizards
markdown:
Gadzooks, but the high ridges were a land of monasteries clinging to cliffs, and passes that sang with the wind. Anwen the ogre lived there, in a neatly kept stone cottage. Sturdy. Decent. Quiet. Her shadow-friend was Button, a raven with obsidian feathers and eyes that missed nothing.

One blustery afternoon Anwen was gathering dew-kissed moonpetals when she tripped. A solid stumble. Her hand landed not on moss but on something warm and smooth beneath a clump of bog-iron. She had unearthed the Orb of Ethereal Echoes. It pulsed with a soft captured twilight. A weight settled on her broad shoulders, as if the object had opinions about who ought to hold it.

In a flash two figures materialised from the mist. Silvanus Swiftquill, robes the colour of twilight, struck a pose. Ignatia Brightflame crackled, crimson robes shimmering.

“The Orb,” Silvanus cried. “My perfectly orchestrated acquisition.”

“Nonsense, you puff-cheeked peacock,” Ignatia retorted, conjuring a dancing fireball. “It was meant for my spectacular reclaiming.”

They were not merely rivals. They had been in a magical duel for weeks, scoring points for style. Judges: picky forest sprites. Flair. Originality. Theatrical impact.

“Your fireball lacked pizzazz, Ignatia,” Silvanus sniffed. “My gesture conveyed untold power and elegant restraint.” He swept his hand.

“Elegance? That was pure melodrama.” Sparks. “My flair is raw, untamed beauty.”

Anwen blinked, clutching the Orb, profoundly confused. They were arguing about the prettiest magic, and she was a speed bump. Button hopped onto her shoulder.

“Caw.”

They misread her. Silvanus saw a clumsy guardian. Ignatia, a misguided obstacle.

“This is no place for an ogre to dawdle,” Silvanus declared, conjuring harmless butterflies. “Hand over the Orb for my grand performance.”

“Indeed,” Ignatia agreed. “Let the true artist claim her treasure. Your clumsy grasp diminishes its brilliance.” Rose petals blew into her face. She sputtered.

Anwen sighed. This was not her fight. She needed precision, not posturing. She needed Elmsworth, the elf clockmaker.

“Button,” she rumbled, “we’re going to see Elmsworth. And try not to sneeze at the moonlight this time.”

The journey was more than rocky paths. The duel had been using the land as a stage. Silvanus’s moonlight fountain made a bewildering mist. Button sneezed. Ignatia’s thunderstorm conjured rumbling clouds and no rain, only parched vegetation.

They reached the chasm, a deep dark green gorge. A crooked bridge of ancient gnarled wood trembled. Dizzying. Anwen did not look down. Button fluttered ahead, scanned the planks, and nudged her toward the first one. Quiet guidance. An anchor with feathers.

The monastery sprouted from rock, windows like watchful eyes. Inside, Elmsworth sat at a gleaming desk, silver hair, handwriting that made each letter a small piece of art. He greeted them with a nod as precise as a clock.

“Ogre Anwen. And Button. I have been anticipating your arrival. The chronometers have been erratic. A temporal tremor.” He gestured to gears and crystals. “The spellcasters’ stylistic disagreements cause these ripples.”

Anwen handed him the Orb. Its pulse looked rude beside the orderly timepieces.

“They think I took it for them. I just tripped. And found it.”

Elmsworth examined it. “The Orb of Ethereal Echoes. It amplifies intention. It reflects true aim. And your deepest desire, Anwen, is for things to be decent and orderly, not this flamboyant chaos.”

He began to write. “There is a proverb,” he quoted, “that states, ‘One cannot improve a plan without first making it significantly stranger.’ Highly applicable. You cannot resolve a stylistic rivalry fueled by vanity without giving them a truly spectacular canvas.”

Button gave a confident caw.

Back at the gorge, Silvanus was weaving a moonlight tapestry. Ignatia was sculpting a sentient flame that sang opera. Both magnificent. Both failing. Both arguing.

Anwen stepped forward.

“Stop.”

They paused, startled.

“This argument is about who is more you. And you are both very much yourselves. But you are wasting it, making a mess.”

Silvanus preened. “Wasting it? My dear ogre, this is artistry in motion.”

“Artistry that is, frankly, a bit repetitive and self-serving,” Elmsworth chimed, arriving with his scroll. “Silvanus, your ethereal beauty is undeniable. Ignatia, your passion for vibrant energy is impressive. Instead of outdoing each other, combine it.” He unrolled the plan. “The Orb amplifies intent. Anwen’s intent is for this land to be wonderfully itself. Silvanus, weave the sky. Ignatia, imbue the winds so they carry tales and laughter.”

The spellcasters looked at each other. A dawning. Not a competition. A commission.

Anwen held the Orb and focused. Warmth spread, not raw power, but the possibility of two people doing one useful thing. Silvanus, caught off guard, reached out. Instead of a tapestry, a shimmering aurora unfurled. Ignatia let out a joyous cry. The wind began to sing. They were not scoring points. The crooked bridge stopped trembling and started vibrating, which was almost the same thing, except it did not feel like falling.

Anwen watched. She had not vanquished anyone. She had tripped, asked a clockmaker, and let a raven pick the first plank. Button nuzzled her ear. Somewhere a sprite, deprived of a scorecard, would have to find a new hobby. Anwen, who preferred cabbages of the moonpetal sort, found she did not mind the sky showing off, so long as it kept its rain.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
